articles.title: Arquibancadas do Círio 2026: Começa venda de ingressos | G1
articles.standfirst: Ingressos estão disponíveis apenas online para setores A e B, sendo este último totalmente coberto. Haverá também gratuidade.
articles.summary: Ingressos estão disponíveis apenas online para setores A e B, sendo este último totalmente coberto. Haverá também gratuidade.
articles.body:
A venda de arquibancadas do Círio 2026 começou nesta terça-feira (8) pela internet. Os valores vão de R$ 150 a R$ 250. Haverá também 900 gratuidades.

⏱️ O Círio 2026 será nos dias 10 e 11 de outubro em Belém . Os ingressos para arquibancadas são para o sábado de transladação e também para a grande procissão de domingo.

Serão disponibilizados cerca de 4 mil lugares para cada dia. A venda é pela Lojinha do Círio .

No momento da compra, o público poderá escolher entre dois setores: Arquibancada A, localizada em frente ao Basa, descoberta, e Arquibancada B, em frente ao Bradesco, totalmente coberta.

⛪ As arquibancadas do Círio ficam na Avenida Presidente Vargas, na altura da Praça da República, e são destinadas ao público que deseja assistir à passagem da Trasladação e da grande procissão de domingo do Círio 2026.

Trasladação (sábado): R$ 150,00 (setor A) e R$ 180,00 (setor B)

Círio (domingo): R$ 210,00 (setor A) e R$ 250,00 (setor B)

Segundo a Diretoria da Festa de Nazaré (DFN), há limite de até cinco ingressos por CPF, com pagamento via PIX ou cartão.

Todos os ingressos serão nominais e terão QRCode impresso, medida que garante maior segurança, evita falsificações e assegura melhor controle de acesso. Não haverá meia-entrada.

Arquibancadas para o Círio são vistoriadas pelo Corpo de Bombeiros — Foto: Alessandra Serrão/Arquivo Agência Pará

A arquibancada começa a ser montada em 15 de setembro. O público contará com área de alimentação, estandes de artesanato religioso e banheiros.

O acesso às arquibancadas será liberado a partir das 17h no dia da Trasladação (10 de outubro) e das 6h da manhã no domingo do Círio (11 de outubro).

Serão 600 ingressos com gratuidade para a Trasladação e 300 para o Círio. O cadastro também será online e deve ser feito a partir de 10 de setembro. Têm direito à gratuidade idosos a partir de 60 anos e pessoas com deficiência.

A retirada dos ingressos ocorrerá no dia 15 de setembro exclusivamente na Casa de Plácido, localizada no Centro Social Nazaré (área do estacionamento da Basílica Santuário), mediante comprovação do direito à gratuidade e apresentação de documento com foto, no dia 15 de setembro, no horário de 8 às 14h. Crianças de até dois anos têm entrada gratuita e não precisam de cadastro.

Lugar em arquibancada é disputado durante procissões do Círio de Nazaré — Foto: Igor Mota / Amazônia Jornal

articles.title: Jovem de SP transforma paixão por velocidade em lição de vida | G1
articles.standfirst: Piloto de Presidente Prudente (SP), Juliana Fuzimotto, conta como a velocidade entrou na rotina e mudou sua forma de enfrentar desafios, com apenas 19 anos.
articles.summary: Trocar o coque e as sapatilhas de ballet pelo capacete e pela adrenalina dos motores não estava nos planos iniciais da família de Juliana Fuzimotto, de Presidente Prudente (SP).
articles.body:
Trocar o coque e as sapatilhas de ballet pelo capacete e pela adrenalina dos motores não estava nos planos iniciais da família de Juliana Fuzimotto. No entanto, o que começou como uma simples curiosidade ao ver o irmão pilotar virou paixão, disciplina e profissão.

Aos 19 anos, a jovem de Presidente Prudente (SP) é um dos nomes promissores do kartismo brasileiro e usa as pistas como uma verdadeira escola para a vida.

A história de Juliana com o kart começou quase por acaso. A piloto, que atualmente mora em São Paulo, lembra que foi acompanhando o irmão em uma corrida que descobriu uma paixão que, pouco tempo depois, deixaria de ser apenas uma curiosidade e passaria a fazer parte da rotina.

O pai havia levado o irmão para correr quando Juliana sentiu vontade de experimentar também.

“Entrou na minha vida quando meu pai levou meu irmão para correr um dia e eu fiquei com vontade. Pedi para ele me levar um dia também. Sempre gostei de adrenalina, então o kart foi só uma ‘escada’”, relata Juliana ao g1.

A primeira experiência foi suficiente para despertar a vontade de continuar. A sensação de acelerar pela primeira vez ficou marcada na memória e fez com que Juliana quisesse voltar para a pista.

“Lembro que quando eu entrei em um kart, eu queria mais e mais. A sensação de acelerar pela primeira vez é inesquecível”, conta a jovem.

A brincadeira, porém, logo ganhou contornos mais sérios. Juliana começou a correr com frequência, treinar todas as semanas e participar de campeonatos. Antes de se tornar uma rotina, precisou também conquistar o apoio da família.

“Nem sempre apoiaram. Na época que eu conheci o kart, eu fazia ballet, e minha mãe morria de medo de eu me machucar. Depois que eu me formei [no ballet] e comecei a insistir, eles acabaram deixando”, relembra.

A jovem pilota Juliana Fuzimotto, de Presidente Prudente (SP), largou o ballet para viver o sonho do automobilismo — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal/Juliana Fuzimotto

A primeira competição também serviu para mostrar que a paixão pela velocidade precisaria vir acompanhada de dedicação. Juliana conta que a estreia revelou um mundo completamente diferente daquele que conhecia e que o resultado não foi o esperado.

“Foi a minha primeira etapa em uma competição, um mundo totalmente diferente do que eu já estava acostumada”, diz ao g1.

A primeira corrida não foi boa, segundo ela. O resultado serviu como um aviso de que, para fazer aquilo dar certo, seria necessário treinar muito.

Foi justamente nesse processo que o kart começou a transformar também a forma como Juliana lidava com os próprios desafios. Entre treinos, derrotas e momentos de pressão, ela passou a desenvolver disciplina e controle emocional.

“Muito treino entre esses dois anos. Disciplina, derrotas e muito emocional, mas entre esse período, creio que cheguei mais preparada”, diz.

As vitórias vieram como consequência desse processo. Juliana conquistou o título do Karteiras em 2024 e repetiu o feito em 2025. Apesar dos resultados, ela não aponta uma conquista específica como a mais importante.

Se as vitórias são difíceis de separar, uma derrota permanece especialmente marcada na memória.

Longe da imagem de alguém que vive apenas da adrenalina, Juliana diz que prefere ficar concentrada antes das corridas. O momento de preparação é reservado para observar, pensar e buscar pequenos detalhes que possam fazer diferença quando estiver na pista.

“Eu gosto de ficar no meu canto, sem muitas distrações, pensando em cada detalhe da pista e como posso fazer para ficar mais rápida”, conta.

Para ela, existe uma percepção equivocada de quem olha de fora e imagina que o automobilismo se resume a acelerar e frear: “As pessoas pensam que é só acelerar e frear, sem pensar na preparação, propósito e as regras por trás”.

A disciplina adquirida no kart também atravessou os limites dos kartódromos. Juliana precisa conciliar os treinos e as competições com a faculdade, uma tarefa que nem sempre é simples, mas que se tornou possível justamente por causa da organização que o esporte ajudou a desenvolver.

“É difícil conciliar com a faculdade, mas com a disciplina que o kart também me trouxe, acaba facilitando”, comenta.

Mais do que aprender a conduzir um kart, ela acredita que o esporte a ensinou a enfrentar situações que fazem parte da vida.

“[O kart] me mostrou que eu preciso ter emocional, preparação e disciplina para lidar com os desafios”, defende.

Juliana também enxerga sua presença nas pistas como uma forma de representação. Ela conta ao g1 que nunca sofreu preconceito diretamente, mas reconhece que outras mulheres já passaram por situações desse tipo no automobilismo.

Em vez de apontar uma única referência, ela prefere reconhecer a trajetória das próprias mulheres que fazem parte do esporte: “Nenhuma piloto em específico [é referência]. Creio que todas as mulheres que começam ou que já estão no esporte, acabam me inspirando”.

Aos 19 anos, Juliana já carrega dois títulos do Karteiras - um campeonato e equipe de kart amador voltado exclusivamente para o incentivo e a participação de mulheres no automobilismo - e se prepara para novos desafios.

Em 2026, entre os objetivos está a participação no Campeonato Brasileiro de Kart, no Speed Park, em Birigui (SP). Para ela, estar no Brasileiro representa colocar à prova tudo aquilo que aprendeu até agora.

O desejo, porém, vai além de uma competição. Juliana já projeta os próximos passos e vê a possibilidade de chegar a uma categoria de Turismo como parte de seus planos.

A transformação provocada pelo automobilismo também aparece quando ela olha para a própria personalidade.

“Mudou muita coisa, meu jeito de enfrentar desafios, entender o mundo e de aceitar que nada vem fácil. Como meu coach diz: ‘prego bom leva muita martelada’”, relembra.

Por fim, se pudesse resumir a própria trajetória até aqui como uma volta de kart, Juliana começaria devagar, aprendendo a pista e ganhando confiança aos poucos. Depois, aceleraria até o limite.

“No começo seria uma volta lenta com muitos aprendizados e uma aceleração constante. Depois, pegando confiança, acelerando até o limite”, conclui.

*Colaborou sob supervisão de Stephanie Fonseca

articles.title: New Hampshire primaries test Trump and the left
articles.summary: President Donald Trump’s endorsement will be put to the test once again Tuesday in New Hampshire’s primaries, where liberal Democrats are also looking to cap an ascendant primary season with additional victories.
articles.body: President Donald Trump’s endorsement will be put to the test once again Tuesday in New Hampshire’s primaries, where liberal Democrats are also looking to cap an ascendant primary season with additional victories. Granite State voters are among the last in the country to choose nominees for November’s elections, and Tuesday’s contests will set the matchup in one of this year’s most competitive Senate races. Trump is hoping his preferred candidate, former GOP Sen. John Sununu, prevails in the primary. On the Democratic side, Rep. Chris Pappas is looking to fend off a democratic socialist opponent for his party’s Senate nomination. A divisive Democratic battle is also unfolding in one of the state’s competitive House seats, which Pappas left open, while another House Democrat is facing a primary challenger from the left. Here’s what to watch Tuesday in New Hampshire, where poll closing times vary by municipality, ranging from 7 p.m. to 8 p.m. ET. Senate matchup Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen’s retirement opened up this Senate seat, and Republicans are hoping to make the race competitive in November. Pappas, who has won in a battleground seat since 2018, is considered the front-runner for his party’s nomination. He already appears to be gearing up for the general election, focusing his campaign on addressing high costs and political corruption and already launching an ad attacking a potential Republican opponent. But Pappas is facing a challenge from the left from Karishma Manzur, a scientist and a member of the Democratic Socialists of America who supports progressive policies like “Medicare for All.” Manzur has sharply criticized Pappas over support and funding for Israel, saying he is “enabling genocide.” The GOP primary includes multiple candidates, but the race is largely between Sununu and another former senator, Scott Brown, who held a Massachusetts seat for three years, previously ran for the New Hampshire Senate in 2014 and served as Trump’s ambassador to New Zealand and Samoa during the president’s first term. But the president backed Sununu, who also has support from Senate Majority Leader John Thune and the National Republican Senatorial Committee. Sununu represented New Hampshire in the Senate from 2003 through 2008 after serving in the House. He lost his bid for re-election in 2008 to Shaheen, but Republicans believe his well-known family name could give him a boost: Sununu’s brother and father both served as governors. Trump lost the Granite State by just 3 points in 2024, giving Republicans hope about making this open-seat race competitive two years later. The GOP has not won a Senate race there since 2010, but New Hampshire does have a Republican governor, Kelly Ayotte. Ayotte is running for a second two-year term as one of two GOP governors up for re-election in a state Trump lost two years ago. Ayotte is not facing any major primary challengers. The Democratic nominee is all but certain to be former New Hampshire Executive Council member Cinde Warmington, who also faces no major competitors and unsuccessfully sought her party’s gubernatorial nomination in 2024. House battles The Democratic Party’s divides are on full display in a primary in Pappas’ now-open seat in the 1st District, which includes Manchester, the state’s biggest city. A crowded field of candidates is running in both parties’ primaries, and the race could be competitive in the fall. Pappas won re-election by 8 points in 2024, but then-Vice President Kamala Harris carried the district by just 2 points. Two of the front-runners are viewed as the most establishment Democrats: Marine veteran Maura Sullivan, the former congressional candidate and former Defense Department official, and Stefany Shaheen, a health advocate, former Portsmouth City councilwoman and daughter of the retiring senator. Two other top Democrats — Christian Urrutia, an Army National Guard officer, and Carleigh Beriont, a union organizer — are running as staunch progressives. Heath Howard, who was backed by the local Democratic Socialists of America chapter, is still on the ballot but dropped out of the race and endorsed Beriont. On the Republican side, Trump and other Republican leaders have endorsed auto businessman Anthony DiLorenzo. He is facing competition for the GOP nod from state Rep. Brian Cole and Hollie Noveletsky, a military veteran and CEO of her family iron company. In the state’s other congressional district, Democratic Rep. Maggie Goodlander is facing a primary challenge from state Rep. Paige Beauchemin, a former nurse who entered politics in 2023. The challenger is running as an unabashed progressive, calling for halting data center construction, new regulations on the artificial intelligence industry, “Medicare for All,” labeling Israel’s conduct in Gaza a “genocide” and abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Although Beauchemin’s campaign is trying to tap into some of the progressive energy that has helped challengers topple incumbents this year, she has struggled to raise money — bringing in $44,000 to Goodlander’s $4.2 million — and hasn’t drawn any outside support from progressive groups. Goodlander is a first-term lawmaker who recently gained national prominence as one of the national security-minded Democratic lawmakers who made a video telling the military that members could refuse illegal orders. She also worked in the Biden White House and Justice Department, and is married to former Biden national security adviser Jake Sullivan. Lily Tang Williams, a former Colorado libertarian who since moved to the state, is expected to win the Republican nomination after she lost to Goodlander in 2024.

articles.title: Key swing state voters to settle dueling Senate primary fights in crucial open-seat race
articles.summary: Karishma Manzur's socialist surge threatens Chris Pappas in the New Hampshire Senate primary as the far-left notches wins across the country.
articles.body: MANCHESTER, N.H. - The Democratic and Republican Senate nominations are up for grabs on Tuesday in swing state New Hampshire, in a race that may determine if Republicans keep control of the chamber in the midterm elections. Socialist-aligned candidate Karishma Manzur is on the move as she tries to pull off a major upset and defeat establishment-backed four-term Rep. Chris Pappas in the Democratic Senate primary. Once a longshot, Manzur gained momentum in recent weeks as the national spotlight turned to New Hampshire after a six-month primary season that saw the far-left score a slew of high-profile victories over centrists in what's been framed as a battle for the Democrats' ideological future. The winner of the Democratic primary will take on either John E. Sununu or Scott Brown, two former senators who are battling for the GOP Senate nomination in the race to succeed retiring longtime Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the first woman in the nation's history elected governor and senator. THESE 12 MIDTERM RACES WILL DECIDE WHICH PARTY CONTROLS THE SENATE Republicans haven't won a Senate election in New Hampshire in 16 years, but they view the open Democrat-held seat as a top flip opportunity in the fight to hold their slim majority in the midterm elections. In the Democratic primary, Manzur is taking the fight to Pappas. "All he wants to do is just get his little cushy job and go to D.C., go to all these parties and these restaurants and just do whatever the bare minimum is," she charged in a Fox News Digital interview. The first-time candidate, scientist with a Ph.D. in biochemistry and nonprofit leader who is a member of a local Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) group, is pushing for universal healthcare, raising the minimum wage to at least $20 per hour, abolishing ICE and ending all military aid to Israel for what she argues is the Israeli government's "genocide" against the Palestinian people in their war against Hamas in Gaza. Manzur charged that Pappas, who has been supported over the years by the pro-Israel lobby AIPAC, is a "genocide enabler." "Chris Pappas has had his turn and has not been able to serve this state honorably. He hasn't done a good job in serving his corporate donors, his AIPAC foreign-aligned lobbies," she claimed. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB Pappas, in an interview with Fox News Digital, said, "Israel's a historic ally of the United States, the only democracy in the region. And you can say that while you have vehement disagreements with the Netanyahu government as I've expressed." Referring to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Pappas said, "I think Netanyahu's being incredibly reckless right now. He faces voters in a matter of weeks and could lose his election. And I think that would be important to set a new tone for the U.S.-Israel relationship." CHECK OUT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POLLING IN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS Pappas, who has been the frontrunner for his party's nomination ever since Shaheen announced early last year that she wouldn't seek re-election, enjoys strong establishment and union backing. And for over a year, as he runs for the Senate, Pappas also takes aim at what he calls a political system "rigged for billionaires." Regardless, Manzur charges that Pappas is taking a page from her playbook. "It's really embarrassing and insulting to the people of New Hampshire. He's been there for eight years. He has not provided any of that sort of populist messages, and now he's realizing, wait, he's dropping in the polls, and now he has to catch up," Manzur argued. Pappas defended his record, noting, "I've been fighting to change Washington to get big money out of our political system since I got elected to Congress in 2018." And Pappas emphasized he's "appealing to those voters between the 20- and 80-yard line on the political playing field, and there are a lot of them in New Hampshire. This is not a left wing or a right wing state. It's a state of voters who are pragmatic." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER While Democrats wage an ideological battle, Republicans are fighting over Trump's influence in their own primary. The president in February endorsed Sununu, a longtime GOP Trump critic, over Brown, one of his first-term ambassadors. Sununu is also backed by Senate Majority Leader John Thune and the National Republican Senatorial Committee. Brown charged in a Fox News Digital interview that Sununu's "got 70 endorsements on his website, but he doesn't have the president’s. He never talks about it. He's embarrassed by it." CHECK OUT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS IN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS "I've had the MAGA base and a lot of those so-called traditional Republicans for almost over a year," Brown highlighted. "Johnny came lately, and he's here, and now he thinks everyone's going to just vote for him. That's not how it works. You got to go earn it." Brown claimed that Sununu is "beholden" to Trump, Thune, the Senate leadership, and outside groups. "He owes them everything. He doesn't work for the people of New Hampshire," Brown charged. But Sununu emphasized, "I'll have one job: stand up for the people of New Hampshire every single day... I don't need to make anyone in Washington happy. It's all about our state, our communities, our economy, and our small businesses." Asked by Fox News Digital about Trump's endorsement, Sununu didn't mention the president's name but highlighted his local endorsements, saying, "We've received tremendous support in New Hampshire ... we've got great momentum at the grassroots level." MEET THE FAR-LEFT INSURGENTS WAGING WAR ON THE DEMOCRATIC ESTABLISHMENT IN 2026 MIDTERMS Trump last week said he'd be heading out on the campaign trail to help fellow Republicans running in the midterms. Asked if he'd like Trump to join him on the Granite State campaign trail, Sununu answered, "I don't need anyone from outside New Hampshire to campaign for me. I've said that from the very beginning." The former senator also disagreed with the Trump administration's trade war with neighboring Canada, saying, "I don't think it's the right thing to pick a trade war with Canada. They're a great trading partner for New Hampshire." In the race to replace Pappas in New Hampshire's 1st Congressional District, Shaheen's daughter Stefany Shaheen, a former Portsmouth city councilor, is in a heated battle for the Democratic nomination against Maura Sullivan, a U.S. Marine combat veteran who later served in the Defense Department during then-President Barack Obama's administration. Gaining strength in the final weeks of the campaign is progressive contender Carleigh Beriont, a Hampton selectwoman. Businessman and auto dealership owner Anthony DiLorenzo, who is backed by Trump, and Hollie Noveletsky, a businesswoman and former state party vice chair who's running a second straight time for Congress, are the frontrunners for the GOP nomination. State Rep. Brian Cole is also bidding for the Republican nomination. In the state's 2nd Congressional District, first-term Democratic Rep. Maggie Goodlander is facing a primary challenge from the left from state Rep. Paige Beauchemin. Lily Tang Williams, a former Colorado Libertarian Party chair who is running a third straight time for Congress in New Hampshire, is the frontrunner in the Republican primary. SCANDALS, SOCIALISTS AND TRUMP ROIL PRIMARIES, SEND INCUMBENTS PACKING AT NEAR-RECORD PACE Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte, a former U.S. senator and former state attorney general, faces no serious opposition as she seeks a second two-year term as New Hampshire governor. articles.title: GOP faces brutal midterm headwinds as Republicans paint election as ‘competition with communism’
articles.summary: President Donald Trump headlines the first-ever GOP midterm convention in Dallas as Republicans fight to hold slim congressional majorities amid inflation.
articles.body: DALLAS — With less than two months to go until the midterm elections, President Donald Trump and Republicans gather in Texas this week for the first ever GOP midterm convention, as they aim to energize the party's base to turn out in key races that will determine if Republicans keep control of Congress. Democrats and Republicans traditionally hold large nominating conventions during presidential election years. But Trump a year ago floated the idea of a similar gathering ahead of the midterms, to showcase the signature policy achievements he and the Republicans in Congress produced the past two years. The president called the convention "a truly Historic Event" and "a RALLY like none other!" when he announced it earlier this summer. Trump will be at the American Airlines Center in downtown Dallas for the convention's Wednesday and Thursday evening sessions. Trump will speak on both nights, and will deliver the keynote address on the first night, with Vice President JD Vance headlining the second night. SPEAKER JOHNSON'S MIDTERM PREDICTION TO BUCK HISTORY The convention comes as Republicans face energized Democrats and stiff political headwinds as they defend their slim House and Senate majorities. There are concerns that the two-day confab that's been described by GOP leaders as a "Trumpapalooza" may not be the best approach with the president's approval ratings deep underwater. But Republicans are expected to paint a contrast, as they use the convention to spotlight the Democrats' leftward lurch and tie the entire Democratic Party to far-left and socialist proposals. "This is not a midterm like any other, because we actually have a competition against communism now, and that's a very serious thing. It's going to animate voters coast to coast," House Speaker Mike Johnson emphasized in a Fox News Digital campaign trail interview last month. Democrats, as they try to win back congressional majorities, were already battling a brand that public opinion polling indicates is extremely unpopular. Making matters worse, the high-profile victories this spring and summer by left-wing and socialist candidates over establishment rivals in Democratic primaries, which gave Republicans extra ammunition to portray all Democrats as extremists. THESE 12 MIDTERM RACES WILL DECIDE WHICH PARTY CONTROLS THE SENATE "What we're going to highlight at that convention is the fact that this is not your father's Democrat Party," Johnson said. "It's a contrast election, and people are making a contrast between common-sense solutions and candidates, and really crazy, which is represented by the other side." But Republicans have their own issues. As the party currently in power, the GOP was already up against traditional political headwinds that have historically led to a loss of congressional seats during midterm election years. Add to that the challenging climate fueled by persistent inflation Americans see daily at the grocery store, high gas prices tied to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran and Trump's negative numbers. "Democrats are going to win back power," Democratic National Committee (DNC) Chair Ken Martin predicted last month at the party's summer meeting as he looked towards the midterms. But his counterpart, Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Joe Gruters, told Fox News Digital this summer, "We have a chance to defy history and win the midterms." DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB The victories by Trump and Republicans two years ago in winning back the White House and Senate and holding the House were fueled by Americans fed up with the high cost of living. Two years later, inflation is the Republicans' biggest liability. Three out of four voters questioned in the most recent Fox News national poll said inflation had caused financial hardship, while 54% expected the economy to worsen. "Donald Trump started a war that no one wanted, and now Americans are paying the price. Gas prices are soaring and families who were already struggling in Trump’s economy are forced to stretch their budgets even further while footing the bill for this war," the DNC's Martin charged. But Gruters and other GOP leaders are spotlighting the major tax cuts on tips, overtime and Social Security that congressional Republicans passed and Trump signed into law last year. "This midterm convention gives us a chance, an opportunity to showcase all the great things this president has done, and this administration, to the American people in a direct way," he said. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER But Republicans are facing a low-propensity problem: MAGA voters who don't always go to the polls when Trump's name isn't on the ballot. Gruters called Trump the "best showman that's ever existed in politics, bar none... He knows how to deliver these low-propensity voters. He knows how to get people up, motivated, excited about the midterms, and that's what we're going to need." Johnson, painting a preview of the convention, told Fox News Digital: "Two nights of earned media on every station in America. We'll parade all of our stars across the stage, talk about our extraordinary record of achievement. The president will look into the camera at the end and say, ‘I am on the ballot,’ because we need his base to turn out." The DNC, which remains in debt and decided against holding a similar convention, sees the GOP confab as a chance to blast Republicans. "While everyday Americans struggle to pay their bills, fill up their tanks, or put food on the table, Republicans are hosting a multi-million dollar celebration to satisfy an aging and erratic Trump and tie vulnerable Republican candidates closer to his failed agenda," DNC Rapid Response Director Kendall Witmer charged. Witmer argued that "Americans don’t want a ‘Trumpapalooza’ — they want lower costs and affordable healthcare." STATE OF PLAY: WHO'S UP AND WHO'S DOWN IN THE LATEST FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS Veteran Republican strategist Doug Heye said the GOP convention isn't a bad idea. But Heye, a former RNC communications director, said "the implementation is important. If it’s Trumpapalooza and 'America has never been hotter or richer,' it will fall flat. If they can be focused on what they’ve done and are doing to lower prices, that, along with fundraising, could have some success." But he cautioned, "everything we’ve seen thus far suggests the focus will be on Trump, not on the issues voters are screaming about." In the midterm battle, Republicans come into the convention with a major campaign cash advantage over the Democrats. "We have a ton of money to spend," Gruters told Fox Business last week. "We have the cash, and we're going to deploy it in a way to make sure that we hold the majority." And Republicans aim to pad their war chest, as they plan to raise millions of dollars this week during the convention. That includes asking donors to fork more than $88,000 for a photo with the president at a private roundtable, according to an invitation first reported by the Wall Street Journal and confirmed by Fox News Digital. Among the other major speakers at the convention: Attorney General Todd Blanche, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Medicaid and Medicare Services Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz, Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner, former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt and Donald Trump Jr., the president's eldest son who's popular among MAGA supporters. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana) will be addressing the convention, but his Senate counterpart, Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-South Dakota), is notably absent from the list of speakers released by the RNC. But a source familiar tells Fox News Digital that Thune will be in Dallas, with a full schedule that includes helping Senate candidates fundraise.

articles.title: The US has a $40 trillion debt crisis. Billionaire Warren Buffett knows how to solve it
articles.summary: U.S. federal deficit hits $40 trillion as interest payments now exceed military spending, raising urgent questions about entitlement reform.
articles.body: America had a headline-grabbing milestone this summer. Unfortunately, it wasn’t our America 250 celebration. Rather, it was passing the $40 trillion mark on our national debt. $40 trillion is a number that is very difficult to get your head wrapped around. It’s more than 120% of our GDP, a ratio that sounds more applicable to an emerging market in crisis than the biggest economy in the world. While the debt in and of itself is a problem, there are two related issues that are critical. One is the rapid growth in debt accumulation. In 2017, we passed the $20 trillion mark, and less than 10 years later, we doubled that to $40 trillion. $50 TRILLION IN DEBT IS NOT A DISTANT THREAT. AMERICA IS SPEEDING TOWARDS IT This begets the second issue, which is the cost to finance all that debt. We no longer have the "exorbitant privilege" as it is often referred to of countries adding U.S. dollar reserves no matter what, and that means now, investors in our debt, if we can find them, are price-sensitive. In layman’s terms, they are requiring more of a premium to lend the U.S. government money. ‘THE ODYSSEY’ REMINDS US OF THE NIGHTMARE WE ARE LEAVING FOR AMERICAN CHILDREN Not only are we running very high deficits (both in absolute terms of $2 trillion a year and in terms of deficits/GDP) that need to be financed, but in recent years, the Treasury has been financing our debt for short-term durations. While a bit cheaper, this debt is in constant need of refinancing (not to mention financing this way tends to be more inflationary). The reality is that the interest we are required to pay on the debt — that is, money we are spending to finance things we have already bought — is larger than our spending on the military and, if things keep going the same way, may one day be the government’s largest expense category. DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS HAVE LOTS OF IDEAS, BUT HOW ARE WE SUPPOSED TO PAY FOR THEM? So, the question that comes up is, what can we do? Is there even a way out of this? The answer is yes. We obviously have the tools to be able to get a handle on our debt. TRUMP TASK FORCE IS TACKLING $250 BILLION IN GOVERNMENT FRAUD. IT’S JUST GETTING STARTED The problem is that we do not have the political will to do so. This is a "both parties" problem. The federal government takes in more than $5 trillion each year. For scope, that is more than the GDP of every country in the world except the U.S. and China, and about the size of the GDP of Germany. WASHINGTON REWARDS FAILURE. IT’S TIME TO SEND CAREER POLITICIANS HOME Yet, our government still overspends by $2 trillion. Despite this, many of those in government refuse to address the rampant waste, fraud and abuse in the system, which estimates put at a quarter trillion dollars to $1 trillion per year. BILLIONS SPENT BY KEY FEDERAL AGENCY HASN'T MADE AMERICAN DREAM OF HOMEOWNERSHIP ANY EASIER: REPORT Congress refuses to take steps to revise our entitlement system in a responsible manner. The reality is that the interest we are required to pay on the debt — that is, money we are spending to finance things we have already bought — is larger than our spending on the military and, if things keep going the same way, may one day be the government’s largest expense category. Because Congress has been so irresponsible for so long, no matter what it does or does not do, Americans will pay the price. But, for politicians, it is easier to blame someone else for enduring inflation than it is to take a political hit over real reform that will have short-term consequences but long-term benefits. JOHN ADAMS MADE A TERRIFYING PREDICTION. AMERICA IS CLOSE TO PROVING HIM CORRECT And that comes to the lack of political will. Nothing changes until Congress changes, and if they are not accountable, they have no incentive to do anything other than pass the buck and the blame. Warren Buffett once said, "I could end the deficit in five minutes. You just pass a law that says that any time there is a deficit of more than 3% of GDP, all sitting members of Congress are ineligible for reelection." I would suggest two changes to this plan. First, change the 3% of GDP deficit target to "any time the budget isn’t balanced," and second, state that it must be done on the cost side, not via raising taxes. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Incentives drive outcomes, and right now, Congress is incentivized in a way that drives bad outcomes for Americans. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP If we want to be able to spend on things that matter (like the defense of our nation), stop the erosion of purchasing power and reset the U.S.’ fiscal and national strength, political will must change, or political incentives must be better aligned with outcomes that benefit Americans instead of the politicians themselves. articles.title: Could Vance’s soccer mom bonus nudge married women back to the GOP?
articles.summary: Every Republican is liable to give you a different answer if you ask them what constitutes their party’s “base.” But from a purely demographic standpoint, it’s indisputable: older, married, working-class white men. The picture of the 2024 GOP electorate from The Associated Press’s now defunct VoteCast (a loss sure to be long lamented) is plain…
articles.body:
Every Republican is liable to give you a different answer if you ask them what constitutes their party’s “base.” But from a purely demographic standpoint, it’s indisputable: older, married, working-class white men.

The picture of the 2024 GOP electorate from The Associated Press’s now defunct VoteCast (a loss sure to be long lamented) is plain about the party’s core: 84 percent white, 56 percent age 50 or older, 53 percent male, 60 percent without college degrees.

That’s not a bad thing for the GOP. There are some problematic policy implications with persuadable voters, like, for example, being too blithe about how things like tariffs and mass deportations would play with the broader electorate.

There are some demographic cliffs out there, too — especially as the college-educated voters become a majority of the electorate in coming years. But if you had to pick a single bloc of the electorate as your core, the archetypal Republican stacks up pretty well against his Democratic counterpart from 2024: an older, college-educated, unmarried white woman.

The two base groups are about evenly matched , but neither is sufficient to win elections on its own, so they have to start adding on. For Democrats, that tends to mean, most crucially, nonwhite voters (34 percent of the 2024 Democratic vote) and younger men (21 percent). The Democrats’ misadventure with Kamala Harris speaks to how even small shifts in coalition subgroups like those can cause a party to founder.

It’s a lesson Republicans may soon learn themselves.

The first and most essential addition to the Republican base is married white women. These voters were about a quarter of Donald Trump’s 2024 total, and as a whole, broke 56 percent in his favor compared with 43 percent for Harris.

If you had to pick a coalition addition, this would be anybody’s first selection. Women vote at a higher rate than men , married people vote at a higher rate than single people and white Americans turn out at higher rates than any other ethnic group . White, married women are the supervoters, with turnout rates eclipsing any comparable large demographic cohort.

Indeed, these voters have been the electoral bulwark for Republicans as the party’s base shifted away from more affluent suburbanites and toward rural and small-town, blue-collar supporters. As was the case when today’s archetypal Republican voter was part of the old Democratic coalition, turnout is a serious problem in midterm elections for populist parties. That’s why Republicans are so focused on base voter motivation this year — plumping for the president in a bro-coded ad blitz and holding a rah-rah convention at a football stadium in bright-red Texas. Even a typical midterm cycle falloff with working-class men would be an epic disaster given the sky-high levels of voter enthusiasm among Democrats right now.

But if Republicans are to avoid catastrophe in 2026, they might be better off focusing on their supervoters.

The midterm electorate is typically a third smaller than in presidential years, but because they are such reliable voters, married white women punch well above their weight in midterms — with 1 in 5 voters coming from that demographic alone. They are the essential ingredient for the new Republican Party, going for the GOP in every midterm cycle of the Trump era.

But not as consistently as their married male counterparts.

If married white women broke for the GOP like they did in 2022, with 56 percent clocking in for the Republicans, it could be the firebreak the red team needs to prevent the worst-case scenario in November. On the other hand, just a small drop, like the 52 percent share in 2018 , would burn Republican majorities to a crisp. And if it’s anything like what happened with white women in the off-year elections in Virginia and New Jersey in 2025 , it would be pure electoral napalm for Trump and his party.

Which may help explain the arrival, timed with the general election kickoff, of a new middle-class welfare program aimed at the GOP base’s political plus-ones. The New York Times got the first look at the proposal from Vice President Vance that would pay stay-at-home, married parents $9,000 a year for caring for their children.

It’s an inversion of the original program, which was part of the bipartisan 1990s welfare reform movement. The idea then was to provide a childcare subsidy to allow parents — often unwed mothers — to complete their educations and enter the workforce. The original idea was about reducing welfare rolls, which it helped accomplish . The new proposal aims to increase welfare payouts to subsidize more traditional family structures.

It’s social engineering that comes as a timely election-year payout to a key electoral group.

The plan, which doesn’t need congressional approval, would be a boon to middle-class families, since most poor families wouldn’t qualify. Only about 5 percent of Americans living at or below the poverty line are in homes led by married couples with children. And since about 80 percent of stay-at-home parents are women, and since the new policy would require the working parent to be employed in full-time work, this is very much aimed at those voters we used to know as soccer moms.

If it worked as a social engineering project, it would have long-term benefits for Republicans. As marriage rates have declined and women have become increasingly economically independent, the number of these GOP-leaning women has steadily declined. In 2016, for the first time ever, unmarried women outnumbered married women in the electorate. The shares have held about even since then, but the long-term trend suggests married women will be eclipsed over the coming cycles.

Efforts similar to Vance’s soccer mom bonus in other countries haven’t moved the needle on family formation or fertility rates — of course, neither have socialistic efforts to provide free childcare outside of the home. People, as it turns out, mostly do whatever they want when it comes to getting married and having kids. In both the left-wing and right-wing versions, the payouts work more like sweeteners for favored parts of political coalitions. Free money, whether in a check or in universal childcare, is always popular — whether that’s for Orbanites in Hungary, democratic socialists in Denmark or tradwives in America.

The Vance plan still has to go through final approval and a brief public comment period, so payouts couldn’t start until next year. But maybe even the promise of a taxpayer subsidy could make a difference for a group of female voters that the very male Republican Party can ill afford to lose.

articles.title: New Hampshire Senate race tightens, Rhode Island governor on track to lose: 5 primaries to watch
articles.summary: New Hampshire and Rhode Island will serve up some of the last major primary contests of the 2026 election cycle, showcasing a likely upset in the Rhode Island governor’s race and bitter battles in the contest for retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen’s (D-N.H.) seat. Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.) and scientist Karishma Manzur will face off for the…
articles.body:
New Hampshire and Rhode Island will serve up some of the last major primary contests of the 2026 election cycle, showcasing a likely upset in the Rhode Island governor’s race and bitter battles in the contest for retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen’s (D-N.H.) seat.

Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.) and scientist Karishma Manzur will face off for the senator’s seat on the Democratic side — a primary that some polling suggests may be tightening. Meanwhile, former Sens. John E. Sununu (R-N.H.) and Scott Brown (R-Mass.) have mounted comeback bids in the race.

The Granite State’s Democratic primary for Pappas’s seat has turned into a war of words between front-runners Maura Sullivan and Stefany Shaheen, the daughter of Jeanne Shaheen, as the pair has traded barbs over nepotism and corporate influence.

Over in the Ocean State, incumbents are trying to fend off serious primary challengers in the Democratic contests for governor and Providence mayor as Democratic primary voters have made clear their largely antiestablishment and anti-incumbent mood.

Here are five primaries to watch in New Hampshire and Rhode Island:

New Hampshire Senate contest down to the wire

The Democratic contest for New Hampshire’s Senate seat is coming down to the wire on Tuesday as Pappas looks to fight off a challenge from Manzur and three other long-shot challengers to replace Shaheen.

Long viewed as the front-runner, Pappas has been endorsed by high-profile Democrats like Shaheen and former Vice President Kamala Harris, while Manzur has picked up endorsements from former Rep. Jamaal Bowman (D-N.Y.) and several Democratic state lawmakers.

Polling, too, has shown Pappas as the clear front-runner , though some has suggested the congressman’s lead over Manzur has narrowed.

Polling from the University of New Hampshire Survey Center released late last month showed Pappas leading Manzur by 13 points. Meanwhile, polling released by the Saint Anselm College Survey Center at the New Hampshire Institute of Politics just six days prior showed the congressman holding a 31-point lead.

There’s been increased scrutiny on the accuracy of polling after surveys overstated Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s expected win against Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) and pollsters’ incorrect prediction that democratic socialist Francesca Hong would easily win the Wisconsin gubernatorial primary.

Manzur has contrasted herself with Pappas by arguing he’s been supported by — and therefore beholden to — special interest groups, including the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC). Pappas’s campaign has argued that Manzur’s campaign has misconstrued how much Pappas has received from the pro-Israel lobbying group and has argued that he doesn’t take contributions from corporations’ political groups.

Pappas’s pitch to voters has been that he has a legislative track record of getting things done in Congress and points to the coalitions supporting his campaign, including organized labor and small businesses.

2 ex-GOP senators look to gain foothold back in Congress

Two former Republican senators are duking it out for the chance to return to their old day job in Washington, D.C., even as all signs point to an easy victory for one of them.

Sununu, who’s served in the House and Senate for a combined 12 years, threw his hat in the race after his brother, former New Hampshire Gov. Chris Sununu (R), declined to run for Shaheen’s seat.

Meanwhile, Brown, who represented Massachusetts in the Senate between 2010 and 2013 before later making two unsuccessful bids in both the Bay State and New Hampshire, is mounting a long-shot challenge.

John E. Sununu is backed by key members of Senate Republican leadership such as Sens. Tim Scott (S.C.), chair of the Senate Republicans’ campaign arm, and John Barrasso (Wyo.), the No. 2 Senate Republican. Polls have consistently shown him comfortably leading Brown by double digits.

Brown, who previously served as U.S. ambassador to New Zealand and Samoa under President Trump, has been endorsed by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo and New Hampshire House Speaker Sherman Packard.

The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report rates Shaheen’s seat as “lean Democrat.”

The Democratic primary to replace Pappas in New Hampshire’s eastern 1st Congressional District has turned ugly and personal between front-runner candidates Stefany Shaheen and Sullivan.

Shaheen, a healthcare business owner, has attacked Sullivan, who served as a top aide in the Veterans Affairs Department during the Obama administration, for her campaign donors.

She has accused Sullivan of taking donations from AIPAC, Palantir and others. AIPAC has become a focal point in the midterms amid the party’s divided opinion over how far to support Israel; Palantir donations have also become a source of tension in some primaries given it’s a contractor for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Meanwhile, Sullivan has hit back, launching an ad that describes the younger Shaheen as a “fancy last name” and accuses her of feeling “entitled to your vote.”

Seven other candidates are also running for Pappas’s seat on Tuesday. Some polling suggests that Sullivan holds a single-digit lead over Shaheen. Cook Political Report rates the open House seat as “likely Democrat.”

A bridge threatens to topple Rhode Island governor’s reelection

The 2023 closure — and slow reconstruction — of Rhode Island’s westbound Washington Bridge has emerged as a flash point in the state’s gubernatorial rematch between Gov. Dan McKee (D) and former CVS executive Helena Foulkes, as the incumbent has received pushback for his administration’s handling of the job.

The bridge was closed nearly three years ago after engineers identified structural issues that they feared could cause the bridge to ultimately collapse, prompting state officials to close a major transit route that connected Providence to East Providence.

McKee has drawn frustration and anger from residents over the state’s slow process to demolish and replace the westbound bridge; he notably did not attend the first press conference where news of the bridge closure was revealed.

Demolition of the bridge finished in December — the governor points out it happened ahead of schedule — and completion of the next bridge is expected by 2028.

“I know there is a lot of frustration, and I accept it,” McKee told The New York Times in a recent interview. “But in the end, people are going to realize we did the right thing.”

McKee and Foulkes faced off against each other in 2022, with the governor edging out his opponent by just shy of 3 points in the primary. McKee has attacked Foulkes over her tenure at CVS and its ties to the opioid crisis. CVS reached a settlement in 2022 to pay states $5 billion for its role in the epidemic.

On the campaign trail, Foulkes has acknowledged that CVS made mistakes but argued that the retailer was “the only chain that cut off over 600 pill mill doctors,” according to The Providence Journal .

“We had an almost 40 percent reduction in opioids under my watch. … What that meant is when someone came to the pharmacy with a prescription from one of these doctors based on the DEA [Drug Enforcement Administration] number, we had to send them away, but they could go down the street and fill it,” she told an attendee at a campaign event, according to the Rhode Island news outlet.

Public polling has shown Foulkes with a healthy lead over McKee. Whoever wins the primary on Tuesday will be the heavy favorite to win in November.

Democratic socialist looks for upset in Providence mayoral primary

Rhode Island could see another incumbent ousted this week as Providence Mayor Brett Smiley (D) looks to fend off a challenge from democratic socialist state Rep. David Morales.

Morales has been likened to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, another democratic socialist, given his social media-driven campaign and focus on affordability. He also enjoys the support of key progressives such as Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.).

Meanwhile, the mayor has leaned on his track record while hitting Morales over previous remarks he made about law enforcement, and he suggested the state lawmaker isn’t introducing new ideas.

Smiley has been endorsed by former Rhode Island Gov. Gina Raimondo (D) — he served as her chief of staff — former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg (D) and Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha (D).

images.caption: A sign directors voters to an entrance for City Hall during early voting for the Rhode Island primary election, Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026, in Providence, R.I.

articles.title: Vulnerable Republicans divided over wisdom of Trump’s midterm convention
articles.summary: Republican senators and candidates have mixed feelings about President Trump’s midterm election convention, with many hoping that Trump can rev up millions of MAGA voters but worried of being tied to a president with a slumping approval rating. Party officials are promising a big turnout of Senate Republican incumbents at this week’s convention, which Trump…
articles.body:
Republican senators and candidates have mixed feelings about President Trump’s midterm election convention, with many hoping that Trump can rev up millions of MAGA voters but worried of being tied to a president with a slumping approval rating.

Party officials are promising a big turnout of Senate Republican incumbents at this week’s convention, which Trump allies will host Wednesday and Thursday in Dallas, but GOP strategists are warning Republican senators and candidates in tough races to stay away.

They say GOP candidates in tough races this fall face a risk in letting themselves get more closely tied to the president only weeks before the election.

“Trump is an absolute albatross for Republicans running in tight races because he promised to focus on the economy and keep us out of foreign wars and the exact opposite has happened,” said a senior Republican strategist who requested anonymity to talk about Trump’s impact on the election.

“By having a Republican candidate attend the convention, you’re tying yourself immediately to the president,” the strategist added.

“You’re already defending a voting record that you may have in the House or Senate if you’re an incumbent and then on top of it, you have to defend anything the president says at the convention, anything anyone else says at the convention, because if you’re there, you’re tied to it,” the source said. “It makes it a lot easier to avoid headaches and issues that your opposition can bring up if you simply [do] not attend and focus on your campaign on the ground.”

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), one of the Senate’s most vulnerable incumbents, has decided to stay away from the GOP gathering in Texas.

A spokesperson for Collins told the Portland Press Herald she “runs her own campaign independent of any national party schedule.”

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.), who may face a tougher-than-expected challenge in a Republican-leaning state, said his time is better spent meeting with constituents in South Dakota and that he won’t attend the convention.

“I’m back in the state of South Dakota,” Rounds said when asked about the convention.

“I do coffees. What I do is I go on out” and meet constituents, he added. “I think I’ve hit 14 different communities since I’ve been back.”

Asked if the midterm convention is a good idea, Rounds said, “That’s up to the folks that want to be there.”

“I’m not going to be there,” he added. “If I got time off, I try to spend it in South Dakota.”

Rounds’s independent challenger, Brian Bengs, released an Impact Research poll of 500 likely South Dakota voters last month showing him tied with Rounds, 44 percent to 44 percent.

While Rounds is widely seen as safe to win reelection, the poll underscores why Republicans aren’t taking any chances in a difficult election year for the GOP.

Trump’s trade war with Canada and his decision to allow the import of 300,000 metric tons of foreign-raised beef into the United States are unpopular with South Dakota voters.

Rounds said South Dakota ranchers viewed Trump’s decision to import hundreds of thousands of tons of foreign beef as a betrayal.

“The suggestion that they bring in 300,000 metric tons of beef is not a popular program. They feel just like the administration pulled the rug right out from underneath a lot of our farmers and ranchers,” he said.

Rounds said Trump is popular in South Dakota and folks “love the president” but “they’re hurt” and feel “let down” by the beef import decision.

A second GOP strategist who requested anonymity to talk about the midterm convention warned that Trump’s low approval numbers among independent voters is a “huge problem.”

“A lot of these close races will be decided by the independent vote,” the strategist said. “A lot of the more moderate Republicans are going to have to rely on the independent vote especially if Trump’s not on the ticket and not as many Republicans turn out.

“The independent vote is always important, but if it’s deteriorating, it’s not a good omen,” the source added.

Republican senators have agonized for months over polls showing independent voters shifting away from Trump and the GOP and toward Democrats.

A Civiqs tracking poll of registered voters across the country shows Trump is underwater with independents in key Senate battleground states such as Maine, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska.

In Maine, for example, Trump has a 21-percent approval rating among independents and a 61-percent disapproval rating, according to the survey. In North Carolina, the president has a 28-percent approval rating among independents and a 65-percent disapproval rating.

In Ohio, the Civiqs survey found Trump with a 27-percent approval rating among independents and a 63-percent disapproval rating, while in Iowa it found Trump with a 24-percent approval rating among independents and a 66-percent disapproval rating.

Still, Republicans facing tough races this fall are hoping that Trump will drive GOP voter turnout and some plan to attend next week’s convention to help generate momentum and enthusiasm among base voters in their home states.

Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.), who faces a tougher-than-expected challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton, the founder of the nation’s largest United Methodist Church, plans to attend the convention in Dallas.

“We’re taking nothing for granted,” said Marshall, who expects Democrats to pour tens of millions of dollars into the race to boost Hamilton.

The Kansas senator said, “We need the president’s base to get out and vote.”

“There may be 200,000 people in Kansas that only vote when President Trump is on the ballot,” he said. “Certainly he needs to communicate to them that he is on the ballot, that if we lose the House it will just be one impeachment after another — his agenda is over with.

“I think it’s real important that he’s able to communicate and get that base fired up,” he said.

Marshall said voters are feeling the sting of high prices, which has become one of the biggest issues of this election.

“This is one of the strongest economies I’ve ever seen, but at the same time people are still stinging from four years of Joe Biden’s inflation,” he said.

“We saw the cost of housing, healthcare, childcare, property insurance go up 50 percent in some four years,” he added, noting the consumer price index — a key inflation gauge — shows prices are rising by more than 3 percent a year.

Even so, Republicans got some encouraging news Friday when the Labor Department reported that employers added 162,000 jobs in August.

Other Republicans in tough races expected to attend the convention include Ohio Sen. Jon Husted and Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers.

articles.title: Ex-DSA member rips Abdul El-Sayed and warns far-left adopting politics of foreign terror org
articles.summary: A former Democratic Socialists of America member warns Marxists and Leninists have taken over the DSA and rips Abdul El-Sayed as dishonest.
articles.body: A former member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) who lives in Michigan issued a dire warning against extremism in American politics, and ripped far-left, progressive Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed as dishonest and "sanctimonious." "So, I think that it's up to everyone to not sit on their hands, Democrats, Republicans, Independents, we all need to be out there," Jake Altman told Fox News Digital. "We all need to be supporting candidates who love this country, who want to deliver for Michiganders. We should not be leaning into this sectarian politics. My fear is we've seen the left wing of the Democratic Party import the politics of Hezbollah into the United States, and now we're living with the sectarian aftermath of that." Altman, who formerly worked for several labor unions, said the DSA began adding fanatical far-left factions, including Marxists and Leninists, around 2014 and 2015. He claimed that at the time, similar far-left actors were taking control of labor unions, intending to use well-meaning workers as pawns in a much larger political battle to push the Democratic Party further left. That was about the time he left the movement, which he said has become "very susceptible to extremist takeover." FORMER DSA MEMBER ALLEGES COMMUNISTS HAVE ‘CAPTURED’ SOCIALIST GROUP, WARNS DEMOCRATIC PARTY IS NEXT "That's not America," he said. "We want... a broad, tolerant America. We want pluralism here. We don't want to be at each other's throats. I'm just — we have to stand up and say 'no' to this." Tensions between the DSA and Democratic Party have reached a boiling point — nowhere more evident than in Michigan — where El-Sayed, who has palled around with socialist streamer Hasan Piker on the campaign trail, is facing difficulty rallying the party's moderates in support of his candidacy. DEMOCRATS' CIVIL WAR HEADS TO MICHIGAN WHERE PROGRESSIVES FACE BIGGEST TEST YET IN HIGH-STAKES SENATE SHOWDOWN "So, I've met Abdul several times," said Altman. "I worked very closely with his dad when his dad was union president of the AAUP local I worked for. So I have, you know, I think I have a pretty good read on the guy." Mohamed El-Sayed, Abdul's father, is an engineering professor at Eastern Michigan University, where he served as president of the school's AAUP chapter and led a faculty strike in 2022. "When I was at the Democratic Party convention, the recent Democratic Party nominating convention, [Abdul El-Sayed] recognized me," Altman continued, clarifying that he was referring to April's contentious Michigan Democratic Party endorsement convention. "He was working a line that I was standing in, and he recognized me, and he asked me, 'why all the hate?' 'cause I had been critical of the campaign up to that point." Altman said Abdul El-Sayed told him that his campaign "doesn't do that," apparently claiming that his campaign wasn't engaged in political mudslinging. EL-SAYED’S HASAN PIKER PROBLEM FOLLOWS HIM TO DEM CONVENTION AS JEWISH VOTERS BREAK RANKS "We see that the guy is not a straight shooter, he's not an honest broker," said Altman. "He, himself, said that his primary opponent, who I was supporting, couldn't string two coherent sentences together. I mean, the idea that he is somehow above it all is just not true. He's the most sanctimonious man in Democratic Party politics, and that's going a long way because there's a lot of sanctimony in that party." As for the DSA, according to Altman, it is unrecognizable compared to just a decade ago. "So, you had this older generation that was very tolerant, part of a broader liberal tradition, engaged in a productive way with the Democratic Party, not a destructive way as we see today," Altman explained. Part of that tradition, he said, was a total rejection of communism. But recently, the party voted to lift its ban on Leninists, allowing the proliferation of extremism among the party ranks. "We've seen in August 2025 that DSA at the convention voted to remove its prohibition on having Leninists operating within the organization," he said. "I mean, it doesn't get any clearer than this." He bemoaned current DSA co-Chair Megan Romer, whom he described as a "Marxist-Leninist" and "fan of the Cuban regime." HOW THE 'LONG MARCH' THROUGH THE INSTITUTIONS LED TO SOCIALIST TAKEOVER OF DEM PARTY: 'NEED TO WAKE UP' Romer traveled to Cuba last year with a group of 40 far-leftists, where she hyped the communist country as "care-focused vs. production-focused," blamed the United States' blockade for the country's food shortages and mass emigration, and said the country has "the most LGBTQ-friendly constitution in the world." Meanwhile, Abdul El-Sayed continues his attempts to try to win over moderate Democrats while also campaigning against Republican former congressman Mike Rogers ahead of the crucial 2026 midterms that will determine whether Democrats regain control of either or both chambers of Congress. Abdul El-Sayed has been dogged by questions about his affiliation with Piker, whom he invited on the campaign trail during primary season. He has refused to condemn Piker, choosing instead to brush him off as a "streamer from California" who has little connection with the Michigan race. articles.title: Netanyahu Was Personally Warned Hamas Was Planning ‘Terrifying Operation’ 10 Days Before Oct. 7 Attack: Report
articles.summary: The Emirati president reportedly warned Netanyahu that Hamas' leader told an intermediary in September 2023 that he was preparing "a terrifying operation."
articles.body:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was warned by United Arab Emirates President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan about Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar planning a major attack, but did not alert his security officials.

The warning about the impending attack was reportedly not passed on to Israel's top security officials, including former Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar and former IDF chief of staff Herzi Halevi.

Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel also separately contacted Netanyahu to warn about Hamas planning "something unusual," but Netanyahu insisted that Israel was prepared for any scenario.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was personally and explicitly warned that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was planning a major attack roughly 10 days before the October 7 massacre , but dismissed the threat and did not alert his security chiefs, according to a shocking new Haaretz report.

The revelations come from research for an upcoming book Hostages: 843 Days of Abandonment , written by journalists Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval , who writes for Haaretz .

United Arab Emirates President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan raised the alarm directly with Netanyahu during a 45-minute conversation, three senior foreign sources familiar with the exchange told the Israeli newspaper, and reportedly warned that Sinwar was preparing a major operation.

Netanyahu reportedly responded that he believed Hamas intended to operate in the West Bank and assured the Emirati leader that Israel was prepared for any scenario.

The warning was apparently never passed to Israel's top security officials. Former Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar and former IDF chief of staff Herzi Halevi both told Haaretz they had not been informed about the conversation.

The report said the Emirati leader intervened after concerns grew in the UAE over intelligence originating with a Palestinian intermediary who had contacts with both Hamas and Israeli security officials.

Sinwar had reportedly warned through the intermediary in September 2023 that he was preparing a "zilzal," or earthquake, later describing what was coming as "the mother of all surprises" and "a terrifying operation."

That intelligence reached the Shin Bet on September 15, according to Haaretz . Bar subsequently briefed Netanyahu and reportedly warned during a security assessment two days later that Israel was "on a collision course," recommending either offensive action or strengthened defenses around Gaza and the West Bank.

Haaretz also reported that Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel separately contacted Netanyahu around the same period to warn that Hamas was planning "something unusual, a terrifying operation." The prime minister, however, insisted again that Israel was in control and reportedly mentioned neither call during an October 1 security discussion about Hamas and Gaza.

The Prime Minister's Office categorically denied the central allegation in a comment to The Jerusalem Post .

"An absolute lie! Prime Minister Netanyahu did not speak with the president of the United Arab Emirates during the period in question and did not receive any warning from him," it said.

Former Israeli Prime Minister Naftali Bennett , however, backed the report Tuesday, telling Tel Aviv-based radio station 103FM he "knew for a fact the report is true."

"Mohammed bin Zayed of the Emirates warned Netanyahu that Sinwar was planning an operation. Abbas Kamel , the head of Egyptian General Intelligence, also warned Netanyahu days before the massacre that a major operation was being planned," Bennett said. "I don't want to talk about my relationship with anyone. I'm telling you that I know this fact is true."

articles.title: Unearthed interview exposes what Talarico thought about 'tough-on-crime' tactics
articles.summary: Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico pushed restorative justice over suspension and expulsion, linking school discipline to criminal reform.
articles.body: James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, once framed disciplinary practices in schools as an outflow of the ideas behind criminal justice reforms he hoped lawmakers would implement in Texas. "I’m recently excited about the formation of a bipartisan criminal justice reform caucus in the Texas House with prominent Democrats and prominent Republicans who understand that we have to move away from a tough-on-crime approach to a smart-on-crime approach, and that, I think, filters down to our schools," Talarico said in a 2020 interview on school disciplinary practices and their effect on minorities. Talarico’s train of thought from criminal reform laws to changes in educational discipline demonstrates his underlying beliefs about moving away from punitive corrections. SOROS NETWORK REBUILDS PROGRESSIVE PROSECUTOR PUSH AFTER STRING OF ELECTION LOSSES Talarico fleshed out his view, detailing how the changes would affect the educational system. "[We are] starting in elementary school, where we really pursue restorative practices that are going to rehabilitate our students who are suffering from trauma, our students who are feeling unsafe in school and our students who harm a classroom community." Talarico was referring to "restorative justice," a view that links misbehavior to past personal and emotional experiences. In the words of Texas Appleseed, a group that promotes "social, economic and racial justice," restorative justice in education emphasizes the relational cost of conflict as a way to deter future bad behavior. "Restorative Justice, when applied to a school setting, focuses on how student behavior has harmed others and how to make amends. Schools use it to build community and strengthen student–school connections," the group wrote in a definition submitted to lawmakers. The approach is often mentioned as an alternative to "zero tolerance" policies that focus on punishments that deter discouraged conduct. To Talarico, its adoption could deemphasize other forms of punishments. "What that means is really allowing students to repair the harms that they’ve caused in a classroom community. It's a lot more rigorous and a lot more effective than just expelling a student or suspending a student or removing them from a classroom community," Talarico said. While in the Texas legislature in 2021, Talarico introduced a bill, HB 62, which would have sought to move schools away from in-school suspension, out-of-school suspension and removing kids to alternative educational programs. The bill stalled in committee and never became law. NORTH CAROLINA TEACHER'S KILLING REIGNITES SCRUTINY OF ROY COOPER'S CRIMINAL JUSTICE RECORD IN SENATE RACE In the wake of the Uvalde school shooting in 2022, Republican lawmakers pushed back against Talarico’s line of reasoning, arguing that, despite some calls for leniency, repercussions for problematic behavior are sometimes unavoidable. "Look, I don't want to see a kid go to jail for being caught with some pot. I don't want to see a kid go to jail because he gets into a fight with another kid," Texas state Rep. Steve Toth, a Republican, told interviewers. "That's clearly not the intent here. But if you've got a kid that is violent and is consistently violent, and they've been violent toward other children and teachers, then we either have to reach that kid or we have to remove that kid. They shouldn't be in the classroom. Period." Talarico’s statements are consistent with past calls to step away from law enforcement and prisons and towards social programs — calls that also show his beliefs about the best ways to deter criminal behavior. "If we took just half of what we spent on wars, prisons, and policing and spent it on education, health care, and jobs, we could make prisons obsolete," Talarico said in a 2022 speech to a graduation ceremony for incarcerated students. A little later on in that same speech, Talarico went further, calling the idea of prisons themselves a kind of violence. "My experience as a teacher, a legislator, and a Christian tells me that birds don’t belong in cages; children don’t belong in cages; people don’t belong in cages. Poverty is violence. Pollution is violence. And yes, prison is violence," Talarico said. MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED FIRES BACK AT CNN CHOOSING TO 'FIXATE' ON 'DEFUND THE POLICE' COMMENTS "I’m not asking you to join the system; I’m asking you to change the system. Dismantle this system of violence." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP When asked about his views on criminal justice and how they link to education, Talarico's campaign said he has always prioritized both safety and smart-on-crime approaches, noting that he had been a member of the state's criminal reform caucus. "James joined his Republican colleagues on this caucus because as a former public school teacher, James cares about keeping Texas students safe. James agrees with most Texans that we government should be smart-on-crime, and our students deserve all the support possible," JT Ennis, a campaign spokesperson said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "While James has passed bills in the legislature to deny bail for violent criminals, crack down on violent felons and send billions of dollars to support law enforcement, Ken Paxton has abused his office to benefit his wealthy donors and the well-connected — allowing criminals back on the street even as it made Texans less safe. Even Ken Paxton’s fellow Republicans have blasted his public safety record: more murders, soft on human trafficking, and pedophiles walking free," he added, referring to Talarico's Republican challenger, former Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Having cleared the primary and secured his party's nomination, Talarico will face off against Paxton in the Nov. 3 general election.
